name: Standard Scramble (First Divide / Marmot Lake approach)
approach: The historic Staircase (North Fork Skokomish) approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and the Duckabush approach described here is cut too: the Home Sweet Home Trail from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide is also closed, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. The Duckabush approach starts at the Duckabush Trailhead via Duckabush Trail #803. The tread starts easy for about 2.4 miles to Little Hump, then climbs the steep, loose-rock switchbacks of Big Hump before mellowing again to the Olympic National Park boundary around mile 6.2-6.7. Continue up the valley past 5 Mile Camp (a popular fishing/camping flat by the river) and 10 Mile Camp (~mile 12), where the trail's grade eases through old-growth forest along the Duckabush River — reliable water the whole way, though treat it. Beyond 10 Mile Camp the trail steepens again through the rougher upper-valley tread toward the Duckabush Camp junction with the O'Neil Pass/North Fork Skokomish Trail; from there it's a tough, sustained climb — the last mile notably steep — up to Marmot Lake (roughly 20-21 miles from the trailhead), a good base camp near Hart Lake (0.9 mi), Lake LaCrosse (1.4 mi), and O'Neil Pass (1.2 mi). From Marmot Lake, drop back to the Home Sweet Home junction and climb the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide (4,688 ft) — closed along with the Staircase side while the Bear Gulch Fire closure stands — then leave maintained trail to angle cross-country/climber's-path up open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Given the mileage (~29 miles one-way), most parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a camp at Marmot Lake (or, once its trail reopens, Home Sweet Home) rather than a car-to-car push.
descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same gully/rib system off the summit rockwall back down through the steepest rock step, then the easier talus and heather below it, back to the basin and First Divide (4,688 ft). This is a scramble route with no fixed anchors or bolted stations reported anywhere on it — the standard descent is careful downclimbing, facing in through the steeper rocky steps near the top where the wall lays back into a short climbable face. Some parties uncomfortable reversing that headwall step opt for a single, short rappel off a natural anchor (slung horn or block — bring webbing/cord, since none is fixed in place) to protect the crux; this is optional, not required, so plan on 0 fixed rappels for a typical descent. Watch for loose rock and rockfall onto any party below in the gully system, and re-identify your ascent gully carefully from above — the same routefinding hazard (many similar-looking gullies and ribs) applies in reverse and is arguably worse on the way down. From First Divide, drop back through Home Sweet Home meadow and follow the connector trail down to Marmot Lake, then reverse the Duckabush Trail #803 all the way to the Duckabush Trailhead (an easier but long walk-out, ~29 miles from the high basin). Both trails off First Divide, the Home Sweet Home Trail toward the Duckabush and the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase, are currently closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire; once the Staircase side reopens, the equivalent reversal drops from First Divide down the North Fork Skokomish Trail instead.

itinerary.cal: Best snow-free window is roughly mid-July through September; an Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required for the overnight camps, and some parties extend to 5 days to also tag nearby Mount Steel from a First Divide camp. The North Fork Skokomish Trail and its camps (Camp Pleasant, Nine Stream, Two Bear, First Divide) are closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, so this plan cannot be followed until the park reopens them.

days.note: From the Staircase Ranger Station (~850 ft) the North Fork Skokomish River Trail climbs gently and steadily through old-growth forest, with several creek crossings, to Nine Stream Camp. This is the easy, graded part of the trip — save energy for the steep push later.
days.title: Approach up the North Fork Skokomish

days.note: A short, steeper day up the valley to a high camp around the unmaintained Mount Hopper Way Trail junction (roughly the Two Bear Camp area, ~3,680 ft). Arriving early leaves time to scout the start of tomorrow's climbers' path before dark.
days.title: Push to high camp below Mount Hopper
days.objective: Reach a high camp near Two Bear Camp / the Mount Hopper Way Trail junction

days.note: The 'Way Trail' is an unmaintained, brushy, route-finding climb of roughly 2 miles and 2,400+ ft from the valley junction to the summit — steep forest giving way to open slopes near the top. Trip reports flag genuine route-finding difficulty, so budget extra time versus a maintained trail.
days.title: Summit day

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Early start for cool temps on the brushy lower climb.

schedule.label: Reach Way Trail junction
schedule.detail: Begin the steep, unmaintained climbers' path.

schedule.label: Break into open slopes
schedule.detail: Forest gives way to more open terrain; route-finding gets easier to read.

schedule.label: Gain the summit ridge
schedule.detail: Short final scramble to the top.

schedule.label: Summit (6,120 ft)
schedule.detail: Views toward the Sawtooth Range and Lake of the Angels.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Descend the same way, watching for the correct brush corridor.

days.objective: Climb Mount Hopper via the Mount Hopper Way Trail and return to high camp

days.note: A long but mostly gentle, downhill-trending day back down the North Fork Skokomish trail to the car.
days.title: Hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day backpack: ~28.4 mi round trip and ~5,300 ft of net gain to the 6,120 ft summit, most of it easy river-valley trail plus one genuinely steep, route-finding summit day on an unmaintained 'way trail'.

pitch_detail.notes: ~13.1 mi, roughly 3,800+ ft cumulative gain via the North Fork Skokomish River Trail through old-growth forest, past Nine Stream and Two Bear camps, to the 4,688 ft First Divide saddle.
Roughly 1 mile east of First Divide; leave the trail and travel cross-country through open subalpine terrain toward the peak's base.
pitch_detail.pitch: First Divide/Home Sweet Home to base of Hopper

pitch_detail.notes: Talus, heather benches, and a short rocky ridge lead to the summit; exposed in sections, cairns are sparse.

waypoints.name: Staircase Ranger Station / North Fork Skokomish Trailhead
waypoints.note: Wilderness permits are reserved in advance and none are issued at the trailhead; parking lot is off North Staircase Road at the end of FR-24.

waypoints.name: Camp Pleasant
waypoints.note: Established riverside camp beside the North Fork Skokomish with reliable water, roughly the halfway point to First Divide.

waypoints.name: Nine Stream Camp
waypoints.note: Last reliable camp and water before the trail turns steeply uphill; gains about 2,600 ft over the next 3 miles to First Divide.

waypoints.name: First Divide
waypoints.note: High saddle between Mount Duckabush/Mount Steel (west) and Mount Hopper (east); the long-unmaintained 'Mount Hopper Way' splits off here toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mount Hopper Way / meadow bushwhack
waypoints.note: The old Mount Hopper Way tread has vanished under brush for over a decade — expect bushwhacking and route-finding through forest before popping out into the open summit meadow.

waypoints.name: Mount Hopper summit
waypoints.note: Final approach is crumbly, exposed scree/talus where the summit ridge narrows and is impassable in spots — pick your line carefully on both ascent and descent.
